name: Marco Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Marco. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the day team on the surgical ward at Westmoor Hospital, mostly hip and knee replacements and some bowel surgery. I start at seven, take handover, then it's getting people back from theatre, checking wounds and drains, and arguing with the bed managers about who can go home. By the afternoon I'm teaching a student how to take out staples without making the patient jump. I like that bit best.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The discharge paperwork, and the phone. Half my day is chasing a pharmacy prescription or a care package so a patient can leave. My feet are wrecked by Thursday. I'm good at the job, they made me team lead at twenty-six, but the pay at Westmoor is lower than in the city.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about home and money.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Lena in a rented flat above a bike shop on Harbour Road. She's a teaching assistant at the primary school, on a contract that gets renewed every summer. We had to replace the car's gearbox in September, so we've got maybe three weeks of bills saved. Westmoor is the only hospital within an hour, so if I want to stay nursing, this is it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I've asked a chatbot to tidy up a rota email so it sounds less grumpy, and once to explain a new blood thinner in plain words for a leaflet. I check everything it gives me. I'm not first in the queue for new things, but I'm not last either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair enough. That's roughly where I'd put my money, if I had any.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and that the real fight in the hospital is still staffing and pay. Online I wouldn't say much. Maybe a joke about all the conference money spent on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit relieved and a bit disappointed. I'd hoped something would take the discharge paperwork off us. If AI is mostly hype, I'm still spending two hours a day chasing pharmacy for a patient who could have gone home at ten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as team lead, keep teaching the students. Lena and I would try to put the money we spent on the gearbox back, a bit each month, by next summer. And I'd still use the chatbot for emails, because that bit works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A low hum of worry about Lena's contract, but that's every summer anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Lena's contract isn't renewed next summer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we're on one wage, and my wage alone covers the rent and not much else. I'd do extra weekend shifts. We've talked about it at the kitchen table more than once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would either of you move for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena's family are here, and she'd hate it. I'd go if I had to, but I'd rather fight for better pay at Westmoor than run off to the city. That's the union in me.

say: The real fight at Westmoor is **staffing and pay**, not AI.
He'd only joke online about **conference money** wasted on hype.
think: He's **half disappointed**, because he hoped AI would take the discharge paperwork.
**Lena's contract** renewal each summer matters more to them than AI.
do: Rebuild the **gearbox money** a bit each month by next summer.
Keep using a **chatbot for emails**, since that part already works.
Take **weekend shifts** if Lena's contract isn't renewed.
feel: **Mostly fine**, with a familiar hum of worry about Lena's job.
S0.quote: If AI is mostly hype, I'm still spending two hours a day chasing pharmacy for a patient who could have gone home at ten.
fieldNote: His own job feels **secure**; the household's weak point is his partner's **yearly contract**.
He's a mild AI user who wanted it to **fix paperwork**.
He'd rather **push for pay** locally than move to the city.

steps.text: Keep leading the day team and teaching student nurses
Rebuild the gearbox money with a set amount each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, checking, planning, booking. That's the discharge side of my job, and it's also a lot of what schools do with the reading groups.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, let it take the paperwork, as long as the time goes to patients. I'd push the union to get a say in how it's brought in. With friends I'd be more worried about the schools than the hospital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my bit of nursing is mostly safe for now. It's Lena I'd worry about. Her school is already trialling a reading app, and she does the reading groups. My job gets easier and Lena's job gets smaller, and we only just cover the rent with both wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to test the new discharge software on our ward, so at least someone who knows patients shapes it. I'd go to the union branch meetings instead of skipping them. And Lena and I would cut the gym memberships and the streaming, and start putting a bit aside straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Torn. Hopeful for my ward, nervous for us at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why volunteer to test it, when you're wary of how it'll be used?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if I don't, they'll send someone from IT who's never discharged a patient. I've seen that before with the drug cupboard system. Better a nurse is in the room complaining early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lena do if her hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's talked about training as a full teacher, but that's a year with no pay, and we can't afford it. Maybe evening tutoring. We'd work it out, but it'd be tight for a while.

say: Let AI take the **paperwork**, as long as the time goes back to patients.
The union should have a **say** in how it's brought in.
think: Ward nursing stays **mostly safe** for now.
**Lena's reading groups** are what an AI reading app could replace.
do: Volunteer to **test the discharge software** so a nurse shapes it.
Attend **union branch meetings** instead of skipping them.
Cancel **gym and streaming** and start saving at once.
feel: **Hopeful** for his ward and **nervous** for home.
S1.quote: My job gets easier and Lena's job gets smaller, and we only just cover the rent with both wages.
fieldNote: The household risk is **Lena's hours**, not his own role.
He joins the rollout to **shape it**, a pragmatic progressive move.
Lena's teacher training is blocked by **a year without pay**.

steps.text: Volunteer to test the discharge software on the surgical ward
Go to every union branch meeting this year
Cancel gym memberships and streaming to start saving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028. Robots by 2031. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments stepping in now: income support, rules on staffing, money for retraining. I'd say it at union meetings and online. I'd say nurses should be in the rooms where these choices are made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the planning and paperwork side of my job goes in 2028, and that's the part they pay team leads for. Then the robots come for the wound care and the lifting three years later. Being the best nurse on the ward stops mattering much if the ward needs half as many nurses by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd sit down with Lena and go through every bill. We'd cut to the bone and save whatever we can before 2028. I'd sign up for whatever campaign the union runs for a basic income, and I'd keep my head down at work and be the person they'd keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. And a bit numb, like when you get bad news on the phone and keep nodding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got three years between AI and robots. What would you use them for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To get as many skills as I can that involve touching people, I think. Wound care, frailty, end-of-life. And to get Lena into something safer, though I honestly don't know what's safe in that picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still plan to have kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about starting in a couple of years. In that world I'd wait. You can't bring a baby into a rented flat with no idea if either of you has a job.

say: Governments must act now with **income support** and retraining money.
Nurses belong in the rooms where **these choices** are made.
think: The **planning side** that pays team leads goes in 2028.
By **2031** robots reach wound care, so the ward needs fewer nurses.
do: Go through every bill with Lena and **cut hard** before 2028.
Join any union campaign for a **basic income**.
Put off **having children** until both jobs feel clearer.
feel: **Frightened**, and numb like nodding through bad news on the phone.
S2.quote: Being the best nurse on the ward stops mattering much if the ward needs half as many nurses by 2031.
fieldNote: He sees his **team lead premium** as the first thing to go.
He'd use the three-year gap to build **hands-on skills**.
Fast AGI pushes back their plans for **children**.

steps.text: Go through every household bill with Lena and cut hard
Join the union campaign for a basic income
Put off trying for a baby until both jobs feel clearer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking side, eight for robots. That's a bit of breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as with the fast one, but calmer: we've got time, so let's use it properly. Fund the training, and make sure the savings get shared with staff instead of disappearing into management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to move into something machines will find hard. I'd look at an advanced practitioner role in frailty care. Five years is long enough to retrain, but only if my employer pays for it, because a thin wallet doesn't fund a second master's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Westmoor to fund an advanced practice course in frailty within the year, and I'd start using the AI tools more on purpose, to understand them. Lena would look for a school role that's more about the children's wellbeing than reading groups. We'd save something every month, even if it's small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but with a plan. That makes a big difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Westmoor won't fund the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look for a hospital that will, even if it means moving away from Harbour Road. Lena wouldn't like it. But I'd make the case to her, and she'd make hers, and we'd decide together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you're not first in the queue for new tech. Would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. With five years, I'd want to be the person on the ward who knows what the tools get wrong. Not an enthusiast, just someone who can't be fooled by them.

say: Five years is enough time, so **fund the training** properly now.
Savings must be **shared with staff**, not absorbed by management.
think: He'd aim for an **advanced practitioner** role in frailty care.
Retraining only works if the **employer pays**, given their thin savings.
do: Ask Westmoor to fund a **frailty course** within the year.
Use **AI tools** more on purpose to learn their mistakes.
Save **something monthly** while Lena seeks a wellbeing-focused school role.
feel: **Nervous**, but having a **plan** makes it bearable.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to retrain, but only if my employer pays for it, because a thin wallet doesn't fund a second master's.
fieldNote: Time turns his worry into a **retraining plan** aimed at frailty care.
He'd use AI to **understand its errors**, not out of enthusiasm.
A move away is possible but a **joint decision** with Lena.

steps.text: Ask Westmoor to fund an advanced practice course in frailty care
Use AI tools at work on purpose to learn their mistakes
Save a small fixed amount every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's nearly a whole career change's worth of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we can actually get it right. Train nurses properly, protect staffing and give people who lose jobs real support. I'd say that at the union and in the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably be fine. By 2039 I'd be thirty-nine and, if I've done it right, working in frailty or community care. Ten years is enough time for me to get ready, but I'm not sure it's enough time for Lena.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still go for the frailty course, but over three years instead of one. I'd help Lena look at teacher training, saving for her year off. And we'd probably go ahead and plan for kids, maybe in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still a bit of worry in the background, but mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why are you less sure about Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because teaching assistants sit right where software is getting good. She's brilliant with the kids who struggle, but nobody pays well for that. I worry she'll be told she's not needed before she's had a chance to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go ahead with kids even with that worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so. Ten years is a long time to put your life on hold. You can't wait for a perfect moment, especially on a nurse's pay.

say: This is the version where we **get it right** with training and support.
People who lose jobs need **real support**, not slogans.
think: By 2039 he expects to be in **frailty or community** care.
**Lena's role** sits where software gets good, so she may run out of time.
do: Take the **frailty course** over three years instead of one.
Save towards **Lena's training year** as a teacher.
Plan to try for **children** in about two years.
feel: **Calmer** and mostly hopeful, with background worry about Lena.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough time for me to get ready, but I'm not sure it's enough time for Lena.
fieldNote: With a decade he's **personally confident**; the worry shifts to his partner.
He refuses to **put life on hold**, a sign of steady optimism.
The slow pace lets him spread **retraining** over years.

steps.text: Take the frailty care course part-time over three years
Save towards Lena's year of teacher training
Plan to start trying for a baby in two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because of me, but because of us as a household. We'd have no time to save and no time for Lena to move. What would help is income support while people retrain, and employers who pay for the training instead of expecting nurses to fund it from nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the students. I teach student nurses every week, and I don't know what to tell a nineteen-year-old about a career that might look completely different by the time they qualify. I'd still tell them to do it, though. People will always need someone at the bedside, for a while yet anyway.

headlineQuote: I teach student nurses every week, and I don't know what to tell a nineteen-year-old about a career that might look completely different by the time they qualify.
portrait: Marco is a 27-year-old **surgical ward team lead** at Westmoor, the only hospital within an hour.
He and his partner Lena rent a flat with about **three weeks** of savings.
He uses AI **now and then** and would test new tools to shape them.
His biggest fear is **Lena's teaching assistant job**, more than his own.
With more warning, he'd move into **frailty care** and go ahead with having children.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because their household would have no time to save or let Lena change jobs.
whatWouldHelp: **Employer-funded training** instead of nurses paying for it themselves.
